Statement 1 correct: new TB case rate **2015–2024** fell **21%** in India vs **12%** globally.
Statement 2 correct: treatment coverage **92%** vs global **78%**.

**2020** amendment: single **SBI New Delhi Main Branch** account; sub-granting banned.
**2024–25**: about **16,200** associations received about **₹22,963 crore**.

26.s: With reference to the 2026 changes relating to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, identify the incorrect statement.
o: State agencies require State approval before conducting FCRA probes.
Revision and appeal lie to the District Judge.
Foreign-contribution-created assets may be subject to provisional or permanent vesting in the Designated Authority.
Registration must specify the purpose and State or Union Territory, while existing bodies must file Form FC-6F.
26.x: The incorrect statement is that State approval is required before FCRA probes. The stipulated requirement is Central approval for probes by State agencies; the other three statements correctly describe the 2026 changes.
26.tq: Negative / Incorrect Statement · tests the “2026 amendment provisions” angle
n: Provisional / permanent vesting of FC-created assets in Designated Authority (vesting concept from FCRA 2010) [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
Revision and appeal to District Judge [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
State agencies need Central approval before FCRA probes [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
Registration to specify purpose and State/UT; existing bodies file Form FC-6F [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
xs: The incorrect statement is that State agencies need **State** approval — option **(1)**; they need **Central approval** before FCRA probes.
Option (2) is correct: **revision and appeal** lie to the **District Judge**.
Options (3) and (4) are correct: **vesting** in the **Designated Authority**; registration specifies **purpose** and **State/UT**, with **Form FC-6F** for existing bodies.
xa: **Renewal** requires utilisation of at least **₹10 lakh** over the prior **two years**.
**Ultimate-donor**, project-wise disclosure is required.
Vesting concept dates from **FCRA 2010**.

26.s: According to the MHA guidelines, what is the correct order when an official programme includes the National Anthem, the National Song and a State song?
o: Vande Mataram → Jana Gana Mana → State Song
Jana Gana Mana → Vande Mataram → State Song
State Song → Vande Mataram → Jana Gana Mana
Vande Mataram → State Song → Jana Gana Mana
26.x: The prescribed order is Vande Mataram, followed by Jana Gana Mana, and then the State Song. The other options interchange the National Song, National Anthem or State Song.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Order in official programmes” angle
n: Order in official programmes with a State song: Vande Mataram → Jana Gana Mana → State Song [July 2026 · MHA guidelines on Vande Mataram and Jana Gana Mana]
xs: MHA order: **Vande Mataram → Jana Gana Mana → State Song** — option **(1)**.
The National Song comes first; the State Song comes last.
xa: **Official Vande Mataram**: **six stanzas**, **3 minutes 10 seconds**; no change in words.
**Jana Gana Mana**: **Rabindranath Tagore**; duration **52 seconds**.
Both adopted on **January 24, 1950**.

26.s:
How many of the following statements accurately describe the FCRA-related provisions and changes?
1. The 2022 amendment raised the limit relating to relatives' contributions.
2. Renewal requires utilisation of at least ₹10 lakh over the prior two years.
3. Ultimate-donor and project-wise disclosure is required.
4. Sub-granting of foreign contribution was permitted by the 2020 amendment.
26.x: Three statements are correct: the 2022 relatives' limit was raised, renewal requires utilisation of at least ₹10 lakh over the prior two years, and ultimate-donor and project-wise disclosure is required. Statement 4 is incorrect because the 2020 amendment banned sub-granting.
26.tq: Count-Based · tests the “FCRA amendment details” angle
n: History: first Act 1976; registration mandatory 1984; replaced by FCRA 2010; 2020 amendment — single SBI New Delhi Main Branch account, sub-granting banned; 2022 relatives' limit raised [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
Renewal: must show utilisation of at least ₹10 lakh over prior two years [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
Ultimate-donor, project-wise disclosure [July 2026 · FCRA — FAQ and Amendment Bill 2026]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **2022** amendment raised the **relatives'** limit.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: renewal needs at least **₹10 lakh** used over the prior **two years**; **ultimate-donor**, project-wise disclosure is required.
Statement 4 is wrong: the **2020** amendment **banned** sub-granting and mandated a single **SBI New Delhi Main Branch** account.
xa: First Act **1976**; registration mandatory **1984**; replaced by **FCRA 2010**.
**Revision and appeal** now lie to the **District Judge**.
**State agencies** need **Central approval** before FCRA probes.

26.s:
With reference to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, consider the following statements:
1. It covers examinations conducted by UPSC, SSC, RRB, NTA and IBPS.
2. Fast Track Courts were first introduced in 2024.
3. The harsher penalty provision prescribes fines up to ₹10 crore and imprisonment up to 10 years for admissions.
26.x: Only statement 1 is correct: the Act covers UPSC, SSC, RRB, NTA and IBPS examinations. Fast Track Courts were first introduced in 2000, and the harsher penalties apply to paper leaks, not admissions.
26.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Examinations covered and penalties” angle
n: Covers: UPSC, SSC, RRB, NTA, IBPS exams [July 2026 · Public Examinations Act and fast-track court for paper leaks]
Fast Track Courts first introduced in 2000 (Centre–State cooperation) [July 2026 · Public Examinations Act and fast-track court for paper leaks]

Union Cabinet approved amendment with harsher penalties — fines up to ₹10 crore and up to 10 years imprisonment for paper leaks [July 2026 · Public Examinations Act and fast-track court for paper leaks]
xs: **1 only** is correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the Act covers **UPSC, SSC, RRB, NTA, IBPS** exams.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Fast Track Courts** were first introduced in **2000**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **₹10 crore** and **10 years** penalty is for **paper leaks**, not admissions.
xa: Introduced in Lok Sabha **February 5, 2024**; in force **June 21, 2024**.
Administered by the **Ministry of Personnel**.
Delhi fast-track court: **Rouse Avenue Court complex**, Judge **Anu Grover Baliga**.

26.s: Under the harsher penalty provision approved for paper leaks, what is the maximum combination of fine and imprisonment?
26.x: The approved amendment provides for fines up to ₹10 crore and imprisonment up to 10 years for paper leaks. The other combinations incorrectly use the asset figures associated with the ADR findings or alter the imprisonment period.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Penalty for paper leaks” angle
n: Union Cabinet approved amendment with harsher penalties — fines up to ₹10 crore and up to 10 years imprisonment for paper leaks [July 2026 · Public Examinations Act and fast-track court for paper leaks]
xs: Harsher penalty: fines up to **₹10 crore** and up to **10 years** — option **(2)**.
**₹118.07 crore** and **₹1,413 crore** are ADR asset figures for CMs; **3 years** is unrelated.
xa: ⚠ CA-360 gives leak involvement as **5–10 years** + up to **₹50 lakh**; organised crime **7 years** + up to **₹10 crore**.
Approved by the **Union Cabinet**.
**884** fast-track courts in **21** States/UTs.

26.s: Under the draft Andaman and Nicobar Islands Tribal Councils (Preparation of Electoral Rolls and Conduct of Elections) Rules, 2026, which electoral arrangement is proposed for each Island Tribal Council?
o: Selection of the Chief Captain only through customary consensus
Nomination of the Chief Captain by the Union Government
Direct vote for the Chief Captain
Appointment of the Chief Captain by the High Court
26.x: The draft proposes a direct vote for the Chief Captain of each Island Tribal Council. The concern raised by Nicobarese leaders is that formal elections could weaken consensus-based customary self-governance; the draft does not provide for appointment by the Union Government or the High Court.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Proposed electoral mechanism” angle
n: Draft: Andaman and Nicobar Islands Tribal Councils (Preparation of Electoral Rolls and Conduct of Elections) Rules, 2026 [June 2026 · Nicobar tribal council election rules debate]

Proposes: formal elections for Village Councils and Tribal Councils; electoral rolls; delimitation; reservation for women; 5–9 Captains per village; direct vote for Chief Captain of each Island Tribal Council [June 2026 · Nicobar tribal council election rules debate]
Concern: Nicobarese leaders fear loss of consensus-based customary self-governance; link to ₹91,000 crore Great Nicobar project [June 2026 · Nicobar tribal council election rules debate]
xs: The draft proposes a **direct vote for the Chief Captain** of each Island Tribal Council — option **(3)**.
Customary **consensus** selection is what Nicobarese leaders fear losing; there is no Union or High Court appointment.
xa: Draft also proposes **reservation for women** and **5–9 Captains** per village.
Concern linked to the **₹91,000 crore Great Nicobar** project.
Councils: **Car Nicobar**, **Nancowry**, **Kamorta**, **Teressa**, **Little Nicobar**, **Great Nicobar**.

26.s:
With reference to the FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. A designated authority appointed by the Centre may manage foreign-funded assets when registration is cancelled, surrendered or expires.
2. Management of a place of worship may be entrusted to another person while preserving its religious character.
3. The proposed designated-authority framework replaces the Section 17 framework.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Bill replaces the Section 15 framework, not the Section 17 framework; therefore, statement 3 is incorrect.
26.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “FCRA Amendment Bill and foreign-funded assets” angle
n: Designated authority (appointed by Centre) to manage foreign-funded assets when registration is cancelled/surrendered/expires — replaces Section 15 framework [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
Places of worship: management may be entrusted to another person, preserving religious character [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: a **designated authority** appointed by the Centre manages foreign-funded **assets** on cancellation/surrender/expiry.
Statement 2 is correct: **places of worship** may be managed by another person, preserving religious character.
Statement 3 is wrong: it replaces the **Section 15** framework, not Section 17.
xa: **Validity**: **5 years**; renew **6 months** before expiry.
Compounding penalties revised under **Section 41(1)**.

26.s: When the Election Commission of India finds a citizenship case doubtful during electoral-roll revision, which course of action did the Supreme Court prescribe?
o: Defer the matter until after the next election without referring it to any authority
Declare the person a non-citizen and permanently cancel citizenship
Refer it to a Foreigners Tribunal under the Representation of the People Act, 1950
Refer it to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955, preferably before the next election in that constituency
26.x: Doubtful citizenship cases are to be referred to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955, preferably before the next election in the constituency. The Election Commission does not itself finally decide citizenship.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Referral to competent authority” angle
n: Referral: doubtful cases go to competent authority under Citizenship Act, 1955 — decide preferably before the next election in that constituency [June 2026 · SC on SIR — ECI can examine but not decide citizenship]
xs: Doubtful cases go to the **competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955**, preferably **before the next election** in that constituency — option **(4)**.
⚠ ECI **cannot finally declare** a non-citizen; **Foreigners Tribunals** figure only in the **Assam D-voter** (**1997**) context.
xa: Name on roll gives only an **evidentiary presumption** of citizenship.
Case: **Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India**.
Safeguards: **Aadhaar** as **proof of identity**; deleted names published with **reasons**.

26.s: Under Section 16 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which person cannot be registered as a voter?
o: A person assisted by judicial officers during a hearing
A person whose name was deleted with reasons published
A person whose identity was established through Aadhaar
26.x: Section 16 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, provides that a non-citizen cannot be registered as a voter. The provision relates to preparation and revision of electoral rolls.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Electoral-roll eligibility” angle
n: RPA, 1950: preparation/revision of electoral rolls; Section 16 — non-citizen cannot be registered as voter [June 2026 · SC on SIR — ECI can examine but not decide citizenship]
xs: Under **Section 16** of the **RPA, 1950**, a **non-citizen** cannot be registered as a voter — option **(3)**.
**Aadhaar** proof, published deletion reasons and judicial-officer hearings are **SIR safeguards**, not disqualifications.
xa: The **RPA, 1950** governs preparation/revision of electoral rolls.
**Article 324**: superintendence, direction and control of elections — ECI.
⚠ Deletion from roll ≠ loss of citizenship.

26.s:
With reference to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. Registration is tied to purposes from a Schedule of 105 permissible purposes, and States or Union Territories of operation must be specified.
2. Proselytisation is excluded from permitted religious activities.
3. The widened definition of key functionary includes only directors and partners.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The definition of key functionary was widened to include directors, partners, trustees, the Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family and others; it is not limited to directors and partners.
26.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “FCRA registration conditions” angle
n: First: amends Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011 — registration tied to purposes from a Schedule of 105 permissible purposes; States/UTs of operation specified; existing NGOs get one year to choose [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
Proselytisation: explicitly excluded from permitted religious activities [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
Key functionary: widened (directors, partners, trustees, Karta of HUF, etc.) [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: registration tied to **105 permissible purposes**, with **States/UTs** of operation specified.
Statement 2 is correct: **proselytisation** is **excluded** from permitted religious activities.
Statement 3 is wrong: **key functionary** includes directors, partners, **trustees**, **Karta** of HUF, etc.
xa: Rules notified **22 June 2026**; existing NGOs file **Form FC-6F** within **one year**.
Extra fee **₹300** per additional objective or State.

26.s: Under the FCRA rules notified in June 2026, which of the following is required to be disclosed by organisations receiving foreign contribution?
o: Only the names of directors and trustees
Only the organisation’s official website and annual expenditure
Social-media accounts, official website, ultimate or original donors and donor-advised funds
Only routed donations received through donor-advised funds
26.x: The disclosures include social-media accounts, the official website, ultimate or original donors even in routed donations, and donor-advised funds. The requirement is therefore broader than disclosure of only the website or office-bearers.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “FCRA disclosures” angle
n: Disclosures: social-media accounts, official website, ultimate/original donors (even for routed donations), donor-advised funds [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
xs: Required disclosures: **social-media accounts, official website, ultimate/original donors** and **donor-advised funds** — option **(3)**.
The other options list only part of this set.
xa: Ultimate donors must be shown **even for routed donations**.
Compounding penalty for admin spend above the **20%** limit: **₹1 lakh** or **5%** of excess.
Diversion of funds: **₹1 lakh** or **30%**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Foreign contribution received under the FCRA may be transferred to other NGOs from the designated SBI account in New Delhi.
Statement B: Journalists are not among the categories barred from receiving foreign contribution.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
26.x: Both statements are false. Funds must come through the designated SBI account in New Delhi and cannot be transferred to other NGOs; journalists are among the barred categories, along with parties, legislators, judges, government servants and media companies.
26.tq: Statement-Based (A/B) · tests the “FCRA account and barred persons” angle
n: Funds via designated SBI account, New Delhi; no transfer to other NGOs [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
Barred: election candidates, parties, legislators, judges, govt servants, journalists, media companies [June 2026 · FCRA rules tightened and FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are false** — option **(2)**.
A is false: funds come via the designated **SBI account, New Delhi**, with **no transfer to other NGOs**.
B is false: **journalists** are barred, along with parties, legislators, **judges**, govt servants and media companies.
xa: Cancellation if inactive **2 years**; re-registration barred **3 years**.
Registration **validity**: **5 years**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026:
1. It changes the name of Kerala to Keralam.
2. The change was approved by the Lok Sabha on 11 August 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on 12 August 2026.
3. The name of the High Court is also changed by the Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: The Act changes Kerala to Keralam, with Lok Sabha approval on 11 August and Rajya Sabha approval on 12 August 2026. The High Court name remains unchanged.
26.tq: Find the false statement by checking the exception relating to the High Court.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Act renames **Kerala → "Keralam"**; **LS 11 Aug**, **RS 12 Aug 2026** — option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **High Court name is unchanged**.
xa: The change is made in the **First Schedule** under **Art. 3**; assent and notification came in Aug 2026.
Another renaming in news: **Nauru** → Republic of **Naoero** (Aug 2026).
AP's **Jonnagiri Gold Mine** became **Swarnagiri Gold Mine** (CDCA Jul 2026).

26.s: The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026, operates through an alteration in which constitutional provision and Schedule?
26.x: The change from Kerala to Keralam is made under Article 3 and involves the First Schedule of the Constitution.
26.tq: Apply the article-and-Schedule pairing technique used for constitutional amendments.
xs: The **Kerala → Keralam** change works through **Art. 3** and the **First Schedule** — option **(3) Article 3 and the First Schedule** is correct.
It was passed by Parliament (**LS 11 Aug**, **RS 12 Aug 2026**) as an ordinary law, not an **Art. 368** amendment.
xa: The **High Court** keeps its old name.
AP now has **28 districts** (since **Dec 2025**; **26** from **Apr 2022**).

26.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment, 2026:
1. It provides 5-10 years' jail and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.
2. The probe must be completed within 90 days.
3. It provides for special fast-track courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statement 1 is correct: 5-10 years' jail and a fine up to Rs 50 lakh. Statement 2 is wrong: the probe must finish within 60 days. Statement 3 is correct: special fast-track courts are provided. So B; A, C and D include the false statement 2.
26.tq: Paper-leak law 2026: 5-10 yrs, Rs 50 lakh, 60-day probe, fast-track courts.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **5-10 years' jail** and a fine up to **₹50 lakh**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the probe must finish within **60 days**, not 90.
Statement 3 is correct: **special fast-track courts** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: It amends the **2024 Act**; assent on **31 Jul 2026**; probes by **STFs**.
It followed **Gen-Z student protests** over paper leaks and the Education Minister's resignation (**25 Jul 2026**).

26.s: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment), 2026, makes insulting or disrupting which of the following punishable?
26.x: The amendment to the 1971 Act makes insulting or disrupting Vande Mataram punishable.
26.tq: Use the exact protected national symbol instead of substituting a more familiar one.
xs: The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment), 2026** makes insulting or disrupting **Vande Mataram** punishable — option **(4)** is correct.
It amends the **1971 Act**.
xa: The Act being amended dates from **1971**; the 2026 change adds **Vande Mataram** to its protection.
Other 2026 amendments: **Transgender Persons** (removes self-determination of gender) and **MMDR** (critical minerals).

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026:
1. It replaced a May 2026 ordinance.
2. It was passed as a Money Bill.
3. The Rajya Sabha rejected it outright.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: The Bill replaced the May 2026 ordinance and was passed as a Money Bill. The Rajya Sabha only returned it; it did not reject it outright.
26.tq: Distinguish ‘returned’ from ‘rejected’ when testing the role of the second House.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the Bill replaced the **May 2026 ordinance** (**Art. 123**).
Statement 2 is correct: it was **passed as a Money Bill** (Aug 2026).
Statement 3 is wrong: the Bill was **passed**, not rejected — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Strength: **34 → 38** (**37** judges + CJI); amends the **1956 Act** (Art. 124).
The LS passed it on **3 Aug 2026**.
⚠ **Art. 123** = President's ordinance; **Art. 213** = Governor's ordinance.

26.s: The protests by Gen-Z students over paper leaks were followed by which development on 25 July 2026?
o: The enactment of the SHANTI Act
The dissolution of the Election Commission
The resignation of the Education Minister
26.x: Gen-Z student protests over paper leaks led to the Education Minister's resignation on 25 July 2026.
26.tq: Connect a public protest to its immediate governance consequence.
xs: **Gen-Z student protests** over paper leaks led to the **Education Minister's resignation** (**25 Jul 2026**) — option **(4)** is correct.
They were followed by the **Public Examinations Amendment** (Aug 2026).
xa: The amendment provides **5-10 years'** jail and a fine up to **₹50 lakh**; probe within **60 days**.
The **SHANTI Act** is a **2025** nuclear law, unrelated to the protests.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about digital platforms under the e-Courts initiative:
1. NSTEP stands for National Service and Tracking of Electronic Processes and provides GPS-tracked summons.
2. The JustIS App is intended for litigants.
3. ICJS links police, courts, prisons, forensics and prosecution.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: NSTEP provides GPS-tracked summons, while ICJS links police, courts, prisons, forensics and prosecution. Statement 2 is incorrect because the JustIS App is for judges, whereas the e-Courts Services App is for litigants.
26.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “e-Courts digital platforms” angle
n: NSTEP: National Service and Tracking of Electronic Processes — GPS-tracked summons [August 2026 · e-Courts Mission Mode Project]
JustIS App: for judges; e-Courts Services App: for litigants [August 2026 · e-Courts Mission Mode Project]
Platform: ICJS; Purpose: Links police, courts, prisons, forensics, prosecution [August 2026 · e-Courts Mission Mode Project]
xs: Statements **1 and 3 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **NSTEP** — National Service and Tracking of Electronic Processes — gives **GPS-tracked summons**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **JustIS App** is for **judges**; the **e-Courts Services App** is for litigants.
Statement 3 is correct: **ICJS** links police, courts, prisons, forensics and prosecution.
xa: NSTEP covers **6,895** courts under Phase III.
**CCTNS**: police FIR to charge-sheet; **e-Sakshya**: digital evidence; **NAFIS**: national fingerprint database.
**Nyaya Shruti (2024, ICJS)**: virtual appearance of accused, witnesses, prisoners.

26.s: Under Section 187(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, what is the maximum total period of police custody that may be sought in parts during the initial period?
26.x: Police custody may be sought in parts during the initial 40 or 60 days, but the total police custody is capped at 15 days. The periods of 40 and 60 days relate to the window for seeking custody, not the maximum custody itself.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Police custody limit” angle
n: Ruling: police custody can be sought in parts during the initial 40 or 60 days; ⚠ total still capped at 15 days [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
Provision: Sec 187(2) BNSS; Rule: Police custody 15 days total, in parts, within first 40/60 days [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
xs: Total police custody is capped at **15 days** — option **(3)** is correct.
It may be sought **in parts** within the **initial 40 or 60 days**; those figures are the window, not the cap.
**7 days** is the extra custody the SC allowed in the AP case (within the 15).
xa: Case: **State of Andhra Pradesh vs Suda Suresh Veera Venkata Naga Raju** — custodial death probe.
**Sec 187(3) BNSS**: detention up to **90 days** or **60 days**, then **default bail**.
⚠ Old **Sec 167 CrPC**: 15 days police custody generally in the **first 15 days**.

26.s: Which one of the following statements regarding police custody and related safeguards under the BNSS is incorrect?
o: An accused may meet an advocate during interrogation, but not throughout the interrogation.
A magistrate cannot impose a blanket condition prohibiting any further extension of police custody.
Police custody may extend to 30 days in total if it is sought in parts during the initial 40 or 60 days.
No person may be detained beyond 24 hours without being produced before a magistrate.
26.x: The incorrect statement is that police custody may extend to 30 days. Section 187(2) caps total police custody at 15 days, even when it is sought in parts. The other statements reflect the rules on access to an advocate, magistrate-imposed conditions and detention beyond 24 hours.
26.tq: Negative / Incorrect Statement · tests the “Rights during interrogation” angle
n: Magistrate cannot impose a blanket "no extension" condition; SC allowed 7 more days (within 15) [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
Section 38 BNSS: accused may meet an advocate during interrogation, not throughout [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
Provision: Sec 58 BNSS; Rule: No detention beyond 24 hours without magistrate [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
Provision: Sec 187(2) BNSS; Rule: Police custody 15 days total, in parts, within first 40/60 days [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]
xs: The incorrect statement is that police custody may extend to **30 days** — option **(3)**; **Sec 187(2)** caps it at **15 days**, even in parts.
Option (1) is correct: under **Section 38 BNSS** the accused may meet an advocate **during**, not **throughout**, interrogation.
Options (2) and (4) are correct: no blanket "**no extension**" condition; **Sec 58** bars detention beyond **24 hours** without a magistrate.
xa: Custody can be sought in parts within the **initial 40/60 days**.
**Sec 187(3)**: detention up to **90 days** (death/life/10+ years) or **60 days** (others); then **default bail**.
Case: **State of Andhra Pradesh vs Suda Suresh Veera Venkata Naga Raju**.

26.s: In the Supreme Court verdict refining the legal definition of ‘industry’, which description is correct?
o: A 9-judge Constitution Bench led by CJI Surya Kant, delivering a 6:3 majority verdict
A 7-judge Bench led by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, delivering a 6:3 majority verdict
A 9-judge Constitution Bench led by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, delivering a 7:3 majority verdict
A 7-judge Bench led by CJI Surya Kant, delivering a 9:6 majority verdict
26.x: The verdict was delivered by a 9-judge Constitution Bench led by CJI Surya Kant by a 6:3 majority. The 7-judge Bench led by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer was associated with the earlier Bangalore Water Supply case and its Triple Test.
26.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Bench composition and majority” angle
n: Bench: 9-judge Constitution Bench led by CJI Surya Kant; 6:3 majority [August 2026 · SC refines legal definition of 'industry']

Reconsidered: Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978) — 7-judge bench of Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, "Triple Test" (systematic activity; employer–employee cooperation; goods/services for human wants) [August 2026 · SC refines legal definition of 'industry']
xs: A **9-judge Constitution Bench** led by **CJI Surya Kant**, by a **6:3** majority — option **(1)** is correct.
**Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer** led the earlier **7-judge** bench in **Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978)**, which was reconsidered.
xa: **Triple Test (1978)**: systematic activity; employer–employee cooperation; goods/services for human wants.
Held: the **1947** definition cannot be applied unchanged under the **Industrial Relations Code 2020**; ruling is **prospective**.

Linking police, courts, prisons, forensics and prosecution

26.s:

o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false

n: Provision: Sec 187(3) BNSS; Rule: Detention up to 90 days (death/life/10+ years) or 60 days (others); then default bail [August 2026 · Police custody under BNSS Section 187(2): SC ruling]

A is true: **Sec 187(3) BNSS** — detention up to **90 days** (death/life/10+ years) or **60 days** (others), then **default bail**.
B is false: **Sec 167 CrPC** allowed 15 days police custody generally in the **first 15 days**; the **40/60-day** window is from BNSS **187(2)**.

26.s:
Assertion (A): Resolutions by a Bar Association refusing to represent accused persons are illegal, unconstitutional, null and void.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

26.s: Under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, what must the court do before proceeding in the absence of the accused?

Automatically acquit the accused, treating absence as proof of innocence
Transfer the case to the Election Commission for approval
Record reasons, with the absence treated as waiver of the right to be present

26.s: In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India, what was the finding regarding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls conducted before the Bihar Assembly elections?

The SIR order was quashed because electoral-roll revision was held impermissible before an election
The SIR was transferred entirely to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955
The ECI was directed to suspend all electoral-roll revisions until after the Bihar Assembly elections
26.x: The case was Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India, in which the ECI’s SIR order was upheld. The SIR was held broadly proportionate, and the ECI was considered best placed to decide the method of electoral-roll revision. The tempting contrary option is wrong because the order was not quashed.

n: Case: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India [June 2026 · SC on SIR — ECI can examine but not decide citizenship]

Upheld: ECI order for Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls — conducted before November 2025 Bihar Assembly elections [June 2026 · SC on SIR — ECI can examine but not decide citizenship]
Held: SIR broadly proportionate; ECI is best placed to decide method of revision [June 2026 · SC on SIR — ECI can examine but not decide citizenship]

It was not quashed, suspended or transferred; only **doubtful citizenship cases** go to the **Citizenship Act, 1955** authority.
xa: SIR was conducted before the **November 2025 Bihar Assembly elections**.

**Article 324**: superintendence, direction and control of elections — ECI.

Statement 1 is correct: ECI may examine citizenship **prima facie and contextually** for the roll.

26.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Special Intensive Revision upheld in ADR v. ECI is correct?
o: The Election Commission cannot examine citizenship in the course of revision.
Exclusion from the electoral roll conclusively declares a person to be a non-citizen.
The Election Commission may examine citizenship, but exclusion from the roll is not a declaration of non-citizenship.
Only the Supreme Court may refer doubtful cases to the Central Government.
26.x: The Court recognised the Election Commission's power to examine citizenship during revision, while clarifying that exclusion from electoral rolls does not amount to a declaration of non-citizenship.
26.tq: Distinguish an electoral-roll consequence from the separate legal determination of citizenship.
xs: The **ECI may examine citizenship**, but **exclusion from rolls is not a declaration of non-citizenship** — option **(3)** is correct.
Doubtful cases go to the **Centre** under the **Citizenship Act 1955** — not referred by the SC, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: The ECI's power flows from **Art. 324** and the **RP Act, 1950**.
**SIR** exclusions are among the year's criticised issues.

26.s: Doubtful citizenship cases arising during the Special Intensive Revision are to be referred to the Central Government under the:
26.x: Doubtful cases may be referred to the Central Government under the Citizenship Act, 1955. The electoral revision power itself is linked to Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
26.tq: Use the statute-specific trap by separating the revision law from the citizenship law.
xs: Doubtful cases are referred to the Centre under the **Citizenship Act 1955** — option **(4)** is correct.
The revision power itself flows from **Art. 324** and the **RP Act, 1950**; citizenship is examined under **s.16 RPA 1950**.
xa: Exclusion from the rolls is **not** a declaration of non-citizenship.
The **SIR** verdict (**Jun 2026**) is among the year's biggest polity events.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding major Supreme Court cases and the creamy-layer principle:
1. Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld OBC reservation and the creamy layer for OBCs.
2. E.V. Chinnaiah (2005) held that any exclusion of the creamy layer among SCs must come from Parliament.
3. Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) held that the creamy layer does not apply to SCs and STs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: All three statements are correct. Indra Sawhney dealt with OBC reservation and the creamy layer, E.V. Chinnaiah referred the exclusion of an SC creamy layer to Parliament, and Ashoka Kumar Thakur held that the principle does not apply to SCs and STs.
26.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Supreme Court cases on creamy layer” angle
n: Case / Article: Indra Sawhney (1992); Point: Upheld OBC quota; creamy layer for OBCs [August 2026 · Creamy layer in SC/ST quotas: Centre opposes]
Case / Article: E.V. Chinnaiah (2005); Point: Any SC creamy-layer exclusion must come from Parliament [August 2026 · Creamy layer in SC/ST quotas: Centre opposes]
Case / Article: Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008); Point: Creamy layer does not apply to SC/STs [August 2026 · Creamy layer in SC/ST quotas: Centre opposes]
xs: **1, 2 and 3** are all correct — option **(1)**.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)**: upheld OBC quota, creamy layer for **OBCs**.
**E.V. Chinnaiah (2005)**: SC creamy-layer exclusion must come from **Parliament**; **Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)**: creamy layer does **not** apply to SC/STs.
xa: **Davinder Singh (August 2024)**: **7-judge** bench allowed **sub-categorisation** of SC/STs by States.
**Articles 341, 342**: President notifies SC/ST lists; changes only by **Act of Parliament**.
The Centre says the **Article 32** petition is not maintainable.

3. An accused who appears later may cross-examine witnesses.

26.tq: Count-Based · tests the “Safeguards and eligibility for trial in absentia” angle
n: Applies only to: proclaimed offender under Section 84 BNSS — offence punishable with 10 years+, life or death [July 2026 · Trial in absentia — Section 356 BNSS]

Safeguards: two consecutive arrest warrants at least 30 days apart; newspaper notice with 30 days to appear; notice at last residence; inform relative/friend; trial only after 90 days from framing of charges; State-appointed defence lawyer; audiovisual recording [July 2026 · Trial in absentia — Section 356 BNSS]
Accused appearing later may cross-examine witnesses [July 2026 · Trial in absentia — Section 356 BNSS]
xs: **Only one** statement is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **Section 84 BNSS** proclaimed offender is for offences with **10 years+**, life or death, not seven.
Statement 2 is wrong: trial only after **90 days** from framing of charges; **30 days** is the gap between warrants and the newspaper notice.
Statement 3 is correct: an accused appearing later may **cross-examine** witnesses.

71.s: Astrobase Space Technologies’ “Everest” engine, unveiled in Bengaluru in August 2026, uses which propellants and is intended for which application?
o: Liquid oxygen and liquid methane; reusable medium-to-heavy launchers
Liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen; reusable medium-to-heavy launchers
Liquid oxygen and liquid methane; submarine rescue vehicles
Liquid nitrogen and liquid methane; reusable medium-to-heavy launchers
71.x: The Everest engine uses liquid oxygen and liquid methane, known as methalox, and is intended for reusable medium-to-heavy launchers. The tempting alternative involving liquid hydrogen changes the stated propellant.
71.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Propellant and application” angle
n: Propellants: liquid oxygen + liquid methane (methalox); for reusable medium-to-heavy launchers [August 2026 · Astrobase unveils "Everest" — India's first private 800-kN engine]

It does not use **liquid hydrogen** or **liquid nitrogen**, and it has nothing to do with **submarine rescue** vehicles.
xa: Unveiled on **7 August 2026** by **Astrobase Space Technologies**, **Bengaluru**.
⚠ India's **first private-sector 80-tonne-class full-flow staged combustion** engine — **800 kN**.
ISRO's **NGLV** is also planned with **LOX-methane**; ISRO is building a **200-tonne** semi-cryogenic engine.

**CODENE** — India's first nuclear design centre — is also at **IIT Hyderabad**.

n: Feature: Stages; Detail: 4 — 3 solid + liquid upper stage (orbital adjustment module) [July 2026 · Vikram-1 — India's first private orbital launch]
Feature: Payload; Detail: up to 350 kg to LEO [July 2026 · Vikram-1 — India's first private orbital launch]
Vikram-S (2022): ⚠ sub-orbital — first private Indian rocket to reach space; Vikram-1 is orbital [July 2026 · Vikram-1 — India's first private orbital launch]
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: Vikram-I has **4** stages — **3 solid** plus a liquid upper stage (**Orbital Adjustment Module**).
Statement 2 is correct: payload up to **350 kg** to LEO.
Statement 3 is reversed: **Vikram-S (2022)** was **sub-orbital**, Vikram-I is **orbital** — so **2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Upper-stage engine **RAMAN-I** is **3D-printed** (tested at **LPSC**); structure is **all-carbon composite**.

71.s:

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both the assertion and the reason are true: helium has atomic number 2 and belongs to Group 18 as a noble gas. However, its group classification does not explain its atomic number, so the second option is correct.
71.tq: Assertion-Reason · tests the “Helium properties” angle
n: Helium (He): atomic number 2; Group 18 noble gas; second-lightest; non-renewable [July 2026 · China's helium export ban]
xs: Assertion is true: **helium** has atomic number **2**; Reason is true: it is a **Group 18 noble gas**.
Being a noble gas does not explain its atomic number, so both true but R is **not the correct explanation** — option **(2)**.
xa: Helium is the **second-lightest** element and **non-renewable**.
It forms from radioactive decay of **uranium and thorium** (alpha particles) and is extracted with **natural gas** (viable at **0.3%**).
Boiling point about **-269°C** — the lowest of all.
⚠ On **10 July 2026** **China** banned helium exports though it produces only about **1.6%** of world helium.

n: Institute: IIT Madras; Development: Alloy Tatvasar AI platform for alloy discovery — LLMs mined 10,000+ papers [August 2026 · IIT innovations — August 2026]
xs: **Alloy Tatvasar**, the AI platform for alloy discovery that mined **10,000+** papers with LLMs, is from **IIT Madras** — option **(4)**.
**IIT Delhi** had **PARAM Pragya**; **IIT Guwahati** the **E-Eye** device; **IIT Hyderabad** the **AnuGyan** programme.

71.s:
Consider the following statements about recent quantum-computing developments:
1. Google’s Willow processor demonstrated that scaling qubit lattices from 3×3 to 5×5 to 7×7 cut the encoded error rate by a factor of two at each step.
2. IBM aims to develop a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.
3. The current era of quantum computing is known as the fault-tolerant quantum era.
71.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Google reported the successive error-rate reduction with larger Willow lattices, and IBM aims for a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The current era is NISQ, or Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum, not the fault-tolerant quantum era.
71.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Quantum computing developments” angle
n: Google Willow processor (2024) — scaling 3×3 → 5×5 → 7×7 qubit lattices cut encoded error rate by factor of two each step [July 2026 · Quantum computing and National Quantum Mission]
IBM aims at fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029 [July 2026 · Quantum computing and National Quantum Mission]
Current era: NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) [July 2026 · Quantum computing and National Quantum Mission]
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Google Willow (2024)** scaled **3×3 → 5×5 → 7×7** lattices, halving the encoded error rate at each step.
Statement 2 is correct: **IBM** aims for a **fault-tolerant** quantum computer by **2029**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the current era is **NISQ** (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) — so option **(4)**.
xa: Willow uses **superconducting** qubits (**Josephson junctions**).
**Quantum Error Correction:** many physical qubits → one **logical qubit**.
Error rates: quantum **1%–0.1%** vs classical one in a **quintillion**.

How many of the following statements about defence systems tested or demonstrated in July 2026 are correct?

2. Ugram is an indigenous 5.56×45 mm assault rifle.
3. Bhargavastra can detect large UAVs at a distance of 6 km.
4. UFOSS is designed to detect only air-independent propulsion submarines.
71.x: Only one statement is correct: Kusha LRSAM underwent its first test on July 23 at APJ Abdul Kalam Island. Ugram is a 7.62×51 mm rifle, Bhargavastra detects large UAVs at 10 km, and UFOSS can detect conventional and nuclear submarines, not only air-independent propulsion submarines.
71.tq: Count-Based · tests the “Missile and counter-drone system details” angle
n: System: Kusha LRSAM; Detail: First test July 23, 2026, APJ Abdul Kalam Island — intercepted high-speed, high-altitude electronic target; against jets, missiles, UAVs [July 2026 · Exercises, missiles and defence tech — July 2026]

System: Ugram; Detail: Indigenous 7.62×51 mm assault rifle — DRDO ARDE + Dvipa Defence India Pvt Ltd (licence 2021, unit near Hyderabad); under 4 kg, range 500 m; passed Army GSQR and MHA tests; likely for CAPFs (CRPF, ITBP, SSB, NSG) [July 2026 · Exercises, missiles and defence tech — July 2026]

System: Bhargavastra; Detail: Indigenous vehicle-mounted counter-drone swarm hard-kill system — Solar Defence and Aerospace Ltd (SDAL); micro-rockets (20 m) and micro-missiles (2.5 km); detects large UAVs at 10 km, small drones 6 km; demo Nagpur, July 24, 2026 (Make-II review, DAP) [July 2026 · Exercises, missiles and defence tech — July 2026]

xs: Only statement 1 is correct: **Kusha LRSAM** had its first test on **July 23, 2026** at **APJ Abdul Kalam Island** — option **(1)**.
**Ugram** is a **7.62×51 mm** rifle; **Bhargavastra** detects large UAVs at **10 km** (small drones **6 km**).
**UFOSS** detects **conventional and nuclear** submarines, not only **AIP** ones.
xa: **Ugram:** DRDO **ARDE** + **Dvipa Defence**; under **4 kg**, range **500 m**; built in **100 days**.
**Bhargavastra** (SDAL): micro-rockets (**20 m**) and micro-missiles (**2.5 km**); demo **Nagpur**.
**Project Kusha:** interceptors of **150, 250, 400 km** range.

71.s: Which combination correctly describes Low Earth Orbit as specified in the Vikram-I context?

n: Global hunger 2025: about 645 million (7.8%), down from 8.1% [July 2026 · SOFI 2026 — food security report]
India: 142.5 million undernourished (down 42% in 20 years); 520.1 million cannot afford healthy diet (cost USD 4.11/day PPP) [July 2026 · SOFI 2026 — food security report]

84.s:

2. Global rice production reached 713 million tonnes during 2010–2015.
3. In 2024, there were 4.9 million deaths among children under five.
4. The annual decline in child mortality was 1.5% during 2000–2015.
84.x: Exactly two statements are correct: global rice production doubled between the 1960s and the 2010s, and 4.9 million under-five deaths were recorded in 2024. The 713 million tonnes figure covers 2006–2015, while the 1.5% annual decline applies to 2015–2024; the 2000–2015 decline was 3.9%.

n: Doubled between the 1960s and 2010s — 713 million tonnes (2006–2015) [June 2026 · Studies — rice production and child mortality]
2024: 4.9 million under-5 deaths, incl. 2.3 million in first month; most in Africa and South Asia [June 2026 · Studies — rice production and child mortality]
Annual decline slowed: 3.9% (2000–2015) → 1.5% (2015–2024) [June 2026 · Studies — rice production and child mortality]
xs: **Two** statements (1 and 3) are correct — option **(2)** "**Only two**".
Statement 1: rice production **doubled** between the **1960s** and **2010s** — correct.
Statement 2: incorrect — **713 million tonnes** relates to **2006–2015**.
Statement 3: **4.9 million** under-5 deaths in **2024** — correct; Statement 4 wrong — **1.5%** is for **2015–2024**; **2000–2015** was **3.9%**.
xa: **2.3 million** of the under-5 deaths were in the first month.
Rice leaders: **China, India, Thailand**; drivers — irrigation, fertilisers, **52%** more area.
**IRRI**: est. **1960**, **Los Baños, Philippines**.

15.s: Which process best explains the formation of beach sand mineral placer deposits along the Andhra Pradesh coast?

Gara and Etcherla carry sediments, while rivers concentrate agricultural minerals
Godavari and Krishna carry sediments, while waves and tides concentrate heavy minerals
15.x: The Godavari and Krishna carry sediments, and waves and tides concentrate the heavy minerals into placer deposits. The other options replace the rivers or the heavy-mineral concentration process with details not associated with the stated formation mechanism.
15.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Formation of placer deposits” angle
n: Northern coast: Srikakulam, Visakhapatnam — Gara, Etcherla, Ranasthalam, Bheemunipatnam, Nakkapalli [May 2026 · AP beach sand minerals hub]
Also: West Godavari, Krishna, Konaseema coastal belts [May 2026 · AP beach sand minerals hub]
Formation: Godavari and Krishna carry sediments; waves/tides concentrate heavy minerals → placer deposits [May 2026 · AP beach sand minerals hub]
xs: The **Godavari** and **Krishna** carry sediments; **waves and tides** concentrate **heavy minerals** into **placer deposits** — option **(4)**.
The other options name districts or villages as carriers and wrong agents (winds, rainfall).
xa: Northern belt: **Gara**, **Etcherla**, **Ranasthalam**, **Bheemunipatnam**, **Nakkapalli**.
Regulation: **CRZ** norms + **EIA**.

1. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is airborne and mainly affects the lungs, though it can affect other organs.
2. Without treatment, mortality is approximately 50%, while four to six months of treatment cures about 90% of cases.
3. The global target is 2030, India’s target is 2025, and the next UN High-Level Meeting is scheduled for 2028.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: All three statements are correct. Tuberculosis is airborne, untreated disease has approximately 50% mortality, four to six months of treatment cures about 90%, and the stated global, Indian and UN meeting targets are 2030, 2025 and 2028 respectively. Each restricted option leaves out one correct statement.
41.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “TB transmission, treatment and targets” angle
n: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; airborne; mainly lungs but ⚠ also other organs [March 2026 · World TB Day 2026 — towards person-centred TB care]
Untreated mortality ~50%; 4–6 months treatment cures ~90% [March 2026 · World TB Day 2026 — towards person-centred TB care]

Global target 2030 (SDGs, WHO End TB); ⚠ India's target 2025; UN High-Level Meetings 2018, 2023; next 2028; WHO Global TB Report since 1997 [March 2026 · World TB Day 2026 — towards person-centred TB care]
xs: **All three** statements are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1: **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** is **airborne**, mainly lungs, ⚠ also other organs.
Statement 2: untreated mortality ~**50%**; **4–6 months** of treatment cures ~**90%**.
Statement 3: **global target 2030**, India's target **2025**; next **UN High-Level Meeting 2028**.
xa: Earlier UN High-Level Meetings: **2018**, **2023**.
**WHO Global TB Report** since **1997**.
**NTEP** runs bidirectional **TB–diabetes** screening; **Chennai** cohort — **34%** of TB patients diabetic.

34.s: At the Hyderabad rally, which measure did the Prime Minister appeal to citizens to follow for one year?
o: Avoid non-essential foreign travel and silver purchases
Avoid all foreign travel and gold purchases for five years
Avoid non-essential domestic travel and gold purchases
Avoid non-essential foreign travel and gold purchases

n: Use metro/public transport, EVs, rail freight; work-from-home; avoid non-essential foreign travel and gold purchases for one year; cut edible oil use by 10%; natural farming [May 2026 · PM's austerity call — forex, gold, oil pressure]
xs: The PM asked citizens to **avoid non-essential foreign travel and gold purchases** for **one year** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The appeal named **gold**, not silver; it was for **one year**, not five; and it was about **foreign**, not domestic, travel.
xa: He also urged **metro/public transport**, EVs, rail freight and **work-from-home**.
He asked for a **10%** cut in **edible oil** use and natural farming.
**Forex reserves** fell ~**$38 bn** in 2 months to ~**$691 bn**.

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

34.x: Assertion A is true: forex reserves fell by about $38 billion in two months to approximately $691 billion. Reason R is false because India imports approximately 89% of its oil; the 75% figure relates to urea imports from the GCC.

n: Indicator: Forex reserves; Value: fell ~$38 bn in 2 months to ~$691 bn [May 2026 · PM's austerity call — forex, gold, oil pressure]
Indicator: Crude; Value: above $100/barrel; India imports ~89% of oil [May 2026 · PM's austerity call — forex, gold, oil pressure]
~75% urea imports from GCC; kharif need 19.4 MT urea vs 5.5 MT stock (early April) [May 2026 · PM's austerity call — forex, gold, oil pressure]
xs: **A is true, R is false** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A is true: **forex reserves** fell ~**$38 bn** in **2 months** to ~**$691 bn**.
R is false: India imports ~**89%** of its oil, not 75%.
xa: ⚠ ~**75%** is the share of **urea** imports from the **GCC**.
**Crude** was above **$100/barrel**; the **rupee** fell below **95 per US$**.
**FII outflows:** ~**₹1.97 lakh crore** (Jan–May).
**CAD (Dec quarter):** **$13.2 bn** (**1.3%** of GDP).

34.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the revised import duty on gold and silver is incorrect?

The Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess was introduced in 2021.

34.x: The incorrect statement is that the measure aims to increase imports and widen the current account deficit. Its stated aims are to curb imports, protect forex, support the rupee and reduce the current account deficit.
34.tq: Negative / Incorrect Statement · tests the “Gold and silver import duty” angle
n: Raised from 6% to 15% — 10% Basic Customs Duty + 5% AIDC (Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess, introduced 2021) [May 2026 · Trade — exports target, CEPA, seafood, gold duty]
Aim: curb imports, protect forex, support rupee, reduce CAD [May 2026 · Trade — exports target, CEPA, seafood, gold duty]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is that the measure aims to **increase imports** and **widen the current account deficit** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The aim is to **curb imports**, protect forex, support the rupee and **reduce CAD**.
Duty was raised from **6%** to **15%** — **10% Basic Customs Duty** + **5% AIDC**; AIDC was introduced in **2021**.
xa: **AIDC** = **Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess**.
Gold imports FY26: record **US$71.98 bn** (**+24%**).
⚠ Gold is the **2nd-largest** import after crude — ~**9%** of the import bill.

34.s:
Consider the following statements:

Statement A: A weak rupee reduces imported inflation.
Statement B: Export gains from a weak rupee are unlimited despite import content and price-taker status.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
34.x: Both statements are false. A weak rupee leads to imported inflation, while export gains are limited because of import content and India’s price-taker status.
34.tq: Statement-Based (A/B) · tests the “Weak rupee and export gains” angle
n: Weak rupee → imported inflation; export gain limited due to import content and price-taker status [May 2026 · Rupee depreciation — to defend or not]
xs: **Both statements are false** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A is false: a weak rupee **raises** **imported inflation**.
B is false: export gains are **limited** because of **import content** and **price-taker** status.
xa: Depreciation also raises the **external debt burden**.
⚠ Higher **FDI inflows** make the rupee **appreciate**.
**Masala Bonds** and easier **ECB** help support the rupee.

34.s:

Reason (R): An expansionary monetary policy by itself does not stop a slide in the rupee.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

34.x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true. However, the composition of foreign-exchange reserves does not explain why an expansionary monetary policy by itself cannot stop a rupee slide; the two statements address separate aspects of the economy.
34.tq: Assertion-Reason · tests the “Forex reserves and monetary policy” angle
n: Forex reserves components: foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, reserve tranche in IMF [May 2026 · Rupee depreciation — to defend or not]

xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A is true: reserves = **foreign currency assets**, **gold**, **SDRs** and **reserve tranche** in the IMF.
R is true: **expansionary monetary policy** does **not** stop a rupee slide — but this says nothing about reserve components.
xa: RBI defends the rupee by **selling dollars**.
Reserves ~**$701.4 bn** on **16 January 2026**.
**Masala Bonds** and easier **ECB** help.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

n: Dornbusch Overshooting Model: exchange rate overreacts in short run (sticky prices) [April 2026 · Rupee as a barometer of credibility]

2. Nicosia is the capital of Cyprus and the euro is its currency.
3. Hanoi is the capital of Cyprus and the dong is its currency.
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: 18 May is to be observed as India–Cyprus Space Day, and Cyprus has Nicosia as its capital and the euro as its currency. Statement 3 is incorrect because Hanoi and the dong are associated with Vietnam.

n: ⚠ 18 May to be observed as India–Cyprus Space Day [May 2026 · Cyprus and Vietnam leaders visit India]
Cyprus: capital Nicosia, currency Euro [May 2026 · Cyprus and Vietnam leaders visit India]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **18 May** is to be observed as **India–Cyprus Space Day** — correct.
Statement 2: Cyprus has capital **Nicosia** and currency **Euro** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Hanoi** and the **Dong** belong to **Vietnam**.
xa: President **Nikos Christodoulides** visited India **20–23 May 2026** — his first official visit.
Ties elevated to **Strategic Partnership**; **2026–31 Defence Cooperation Roadmap**.

66.s:
In the context of the 1973 Oil Price Crisis and the present Strait of Hormuz disruption, consider the following statements:
1. The 1973 crisis involved a political oil embargo.
2. The present crisis involves physical disruption of supply routes.
3. India approached the IMF after the 1973 crisis rather than after the 1979 crisis.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 1973 crisis was a political embargo, whereas the present crisis involves physical disruption of supply routes. Statement 3 is incorrect because India approached the IMF after the 1979 crisis, not after the 1973 crisis.
66.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Political embargo versus physical disruption” angle
n: ⚠ 1973 = political embargo; present crisis = physical disruption of supply routes [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
1979: Iranian Revolution; prices $13 (1979) → ~$34 (1980); India's BoP crisis → ⚠ approached IMF after 1979 (not 1973) [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(3)**.
1973 was a **political embargo**; the present crisis is **physical disruption** of supply routes.
Statement 3 is wrong: India approached the **IMF** after **1979**, not 1973.
xa: **1979** crisis: **Iranian Revolution**; prices **$13 (1979) → ~$34 (1980)**; India's **BoP crisis**.
**1973**: India's oil import bill **$500 million (1973) → $1.3 billion (1974)**; inflation ~**20%**.
The 1973 shock upset the **Fifth Five-Year Plan** assumptions.

66.s: The Strait of Hormuz, central to the disruption of oil flows discussed in April 2026, lies between which two areas?
o: Southern Chile and the Pacific Ocean
66.x: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman, linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. Yemen and Djibouti are associated with Bab-el-Mandeb, while the other options refer to different maritime locations.
66.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Strategic maritime location” angle
n: Strait of Hormuz: between Iran and Oman (Musandam); links Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman; ~33 km at narrowest; ~one-fifth of global petroleum; Qatar LNG; ⚠ no direct link to Red Sea [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
Bab-el-Mandeb: Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea — Red Sea ↔ Gulf of Aden [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
Bosphorus: within Turkey — Black Sea ↔ Sea of Marmara; Magellan: southern Chile [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
xs: The Strait of Hormuz lies between **Iran** and **Oman** — option **(4)**.
**Yemen and Djibouti** flank **Bab-el-Mandeb**; **Bosphorus** is within **Turkey**; **Magellan** is in southern **Chile**.
xa: Hormuz links the **Persian Gulf** and **Gulf of Oman**; ~**33 km** at narrowest.
It carries ~**one-fifth** of global petroleum and **Qatar LNG**.
⚠ Hormuz has no direct link to the **Red Sea**.

66.s:
With reference to Chabahar, the International North–South Transport Corridor and CAATSA, consider the following statements:
1. Chabahar is outside the Persian Gulf.
2. The Shahid Beheshti terminal is run by India Ports Global Limited under a 10-year agreement signed in May 2024.
3. The International North–South Transport Corridor includes Southeast Asia.
4. CAATSA concerns Russia, Iran and North Korea.

How many of the above statements are correct?
66.x: Only three statements are correct: Statements 1, 2 and 4 accurately describe Chabahar, the Shahid Beheshti terminal and CAATSA. Statement 3 is incorrect because the 7,200-kilometre International North–South Transport Corridor covers India, Iran, Russia, Central Asia and Europe, not Southeast Asia.
66.tq: Count-Based · tests the “Chabahar and INSTC” angle
n: CAATSA: Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act, 2017 — Russia, Iran, North Korea [April 2026 · US unilateral sanctions, CAATSA and Chabahar]
Chabahar: south-eastern Iran on Gulf of Oman — ⚠ outside Persian Gulf; Iran's only oceanic port; counter to Gwadar (Pakistan) [April 2026 · US unilateral sanctions, CAATSA and Chabahar]
Shahid Beheshti terminal run by India Ports Global Limited (IPGL) — 10-year agreement (May 2024) [April 2026 · US unilateral sanctions, CAATSA and Chabahar]
INSTC: 7,200 km multimodal — India, Iran, Russia, Central Asia, Europe (⚠ not Southeast Asia) [April 2026 · US unilateral sanctions, CAATSA and Chabahar]
xs: **Only three** statements (1, 2 and 4) are correct — option **(3)**.
1: **Chabahar** is on the **Gulf of Oman** — ⚠ **outside** the Persian Gulf; 2: **Shahid Beheshti terminal** run by **IPGL** under a **10-year** agreement (**May 2024**).
4: **CAATSA** covers **Russia, Iran, North Korea** — correct.
3 is wrong: the **7,200 km INSTC** links India, Iran, Russia, Central Asia, Europe — ⚠ not Southeast Asia.
xa: Chabahar is Iran's only oceanic port — a counter to **Gwadar** (Pakistan).
India stopped **Iranian oil** after **2019** sanctions.
The **US waiver for Chabahar** was nearing expiry.

xs: It was the ⚠ **first bilateral visit at this level** — option **(2)**.

Gulf of Aden, Persian Gulf and Bab-el-Mandeb
Suez Canal, Gulf of Oman and Bab-el-Mandeb

n: Connected to Red Sea: Gulf of Aden, Suez Canal, Bab-el-Mandeb [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
xs: **Gulf of Aden, Suez Canal and Bab-el-Mandeb** are connected to the Red Sea — option **(1)**.

66.s: During Iran's selective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, passage was announced for which group of countries?
o: The United States, Israel and their allies
India, China, Russia, Iraq and Pakistan
Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE
66.x: Iran announced passage for India, China, Russia, Iraq and Pakistan, describing them as friendly nations. The United States, Israel and their allies were in the group for which the strait was closed.
66.tq: Direct Recall · tests the “Permission for passage” angle
n: Amid the US–Israel–Iran war (2026), Iran imposed a selective blockade — closed for US, Israel and allies; open to "friendly nations" India, China, Russia, Iraq, Pakistan [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]

Iran FM Seyyed Abbas Araghchi announced passage for India, China, Russia, Iraq, Pakistan; Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
xs: Iran announced passage for **India, China, Russia, Iraq and Pakistan** — option **(2)**.
Iran FM **Seyyed Abbas Araghchi** announced it; the strait was closed for the **US, Israel and allies**.
**Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE** are the strait's users; **Hezbollah, Hamas, Houthis** form the **Axis of Resistance**.
xa: **Traffic**: ~**130 ships/day** before → **3–4/day**; **20+** vessels attacked; ~**2,000** stranded.
**Toll-booth system**: up to **$2 million per ship**, some in **yuan** (Iran denies).
⚠ India's ships passed with **no formal agreement** and **no payments**.
Iran President: **Masoud Pezeshkian**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about the Strait of Hormuz:

1. It lies between Iran to the north and Oman and the UAE to the south.
2. It links the Persian Gulf with the Arabian Sea.
3. Its narrowest point is approximately 50 km wide.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the strait lies between Iran and Oman and the UAE, and links the Persian Gulf with the Arabian Sea. Statement 3 is incorrect because approximately 50 km is its width at entry, while its narrowest point is approximately 33 km.
66.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Geography of the Strait of Hormuz” angle
n: Between Iran (north) and Oman & UAE (south); links Persian Gulf → Arabian Sea [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
Width ~50 km at entry, ~33 km narrowest; ~20 mb/d (~20% of oil trade); ~$600 billion a year [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(2)**.
1: Hormuz lies between **Iran (north)** and **Oman & UAE (south)**; 2: it links the **Persian Gulf → Arabian Sea**.
3 is wrong: ~**50 km** is the width at entry; the narrowest point is ~**33 km**.
xa: It carries ~**20 mb/d** (~**20%** of oil trade), worth ~**$600 billion** a year.
The Gulf produces **22%** of global oil.
⚠ Natural straits — **no tolls**; artificial canals (**Suez**, **Panama**) charge fees.

66.x: The Manas joins the Brahmaputra. Sankosh forms a boundary in stretches, while Wang Chhu and Punatsangchhu are other rivers listed in the border-rivers cooperation context.

66.s: Which one of the following statements about Indian ships using the Strait of Hormuz during the crisis is incorrect?
o: India had a formal agreement with Iran covering passage through the strait
Pine Gas, Jag Vasant, Shivalik, Nanda Devi and Jag Laadki were among the Indian ships using the route
India made no payments for passage through the strait
The listed Indian ships used the Hormuz route
66.x: The incorrect statement is that India had a formal agreement with Iran. The fact specifies that there was no formal agreement and no payments, although the listed Indian ships used the route.
66.tq: Negative / Incorrect Statement · tests the “Indian ships and formal agreement” angle
n: India: ships via Hormuz incl. Pine Gas, Jag Vasant, Shivalik, Nanda Devi, Jag Laadki; ⚠ no formal agreement, no payments [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
xs: The incorrect statement is that India had a **formal agreement** with Iran — option **(1)**.
⚠ India's ships passed with **no formal agreement** and **no payments**.
**Pine Gas**, **Jag Vasant**, **Shivalik**, **Nanda Devi**, **Jag Laadki** did use the route.
xa: Iran's **selective blockade** closed the strait for **US, Israel and allies**.
**Toll-booth system**: vetting, clearance code, escort; up to **$2 million per ship**.
The **GCC** called the tolls a clear violation.

66.s:
Match the following UNCLOS provisions with the relevant legal position concerning passage through a strait:

List-I
(a) Article 38
(b) Article 39
(c) Article 44
(d) Natural straits

List-II
(i) Duties of ships during passage
(ii) No tolls
(iii) Right of transit passage
(iv) Coastal States cannot suspend or hamper passage

Select the correct answer using the codes below.
66.x: The correct pairs are Article 38–right of transit passage, Article 39–duties of ships, Article 44–coastal States cannot suspend or hamper passage, and natural straits–no tolls. The other codes interchange these legal provisions.
66.tq: List-Matching · tests the “UNCLOS provisions” angle
n: Article: Article 38; Provision: Right of transit passage [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
Article: Article 39; Provision: Duties of ships during passage [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
Article: Article 44; Provision: Coastal states cannot suspend/hamper passage [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
⚠ Natural straits — no tolls; artificial canals (Suez, Panama) charge fees; GCC called it a clear violation [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
xs: Correct code: **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(2)**.
**Article 38** — right of **transit passage**; **Article 39** — duties of ships during passage.
**Article 44** — coastal states cannot suspend/hamper passage; **natural straits** — **no tolls**.
xa: Artificial canals (**Suez**, **Panama**) charge fees.
The **GCC** called Iran's tolls a clear violation.
**UNCLOS** adopted **10 December 1982** at **Montego Bay**.

n: Axis of Resistance: Hezbollah (Lebanon), Hamas (Gaza), Houthis (Yemen) [March 2026 · US–Israel attack on Iran and Strait of Hormuz risks]
JCPOA (2015): P5+1, EU and Iran; ⚠ US withdrew in 2018 [March 2026 · US–Israel attack on Iran and Strait of Hormuz risks]
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct: option **(1)**.

2: **JCPOA (2015)** — **P5+1**, **EU** and Iran; 3: ⚠ **US withdrew in 2018**.

66.s:
With reference to the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, consider the following statements:

1. It links the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
2. Around 20% of global oil and LNG trade passes through it.
3. India imports 85% or more of its LNG through the Strait of Hormuz.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Strait links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and handles around 20% of global oil and LNG trade. Statement 3 is incorrect because India imports 85% or more of its crude, not LNG, through this context. Therefore, the correct answer is 1 and 2 only.
66.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Strategic importance of Strait of Hormuz” angle
n: Hormuz links the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman; ~20% of global oil and LNG trade; India imports 85%+ of crude [March 2026 · Strait of Hormuz crisis — Iran's selective blockade and toll system]
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: Hormuz links the **Persian Gulf** and **Gulf of Oman**; 2: ~**20%** of global oil and LNG trade.
3 is wrong: India imports **85%+** of its **crude**, not LNG; ~**60% of LNG** imports transit Hormuz.
xa: **80–85% of LPG** imports transit Hormuz.
⚠ India lacks large strategic reserves for **LPG/LNG**.
Width ~**33 km** at narrowest.

66.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India is exploring uranium across 15 states, and a Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is located at Kalpakkam.
2. CIRUS was India's second reactor in the 1950s, while RAPP was associated with Rajasthan in the 1960s.
3. Uranium has atomic number 92, and U-235 is fissile while U-238 is fertile.
66.x: All three statements are correct: exploration covers 15 states, the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is at Kalpakkam, CIRUS and RAPP belong to the stated periods, and uranium has atomic number 92 with U-235 fissile and U-238 fertile. The other options omit one or more correct statements.
66.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Nuclear programme and uranium background” angle
n: Exploration across 15 states; Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam [March 2026 · India–Canada: Carney visit, Cameco uranium deal and agreements]
CIRUS (Canada India Reactor Utility Service) — India's second reactor, 1950s; RAPP (Rajasthan) in 1960s [March 2026 · India–Canada: Carney visit, Cameco uranium deal and agreements]
Uranium: atomic number 92, mass ~238 u; ore Uraninite (Pitchblende); U-238 ~99.3% (fertile), U-235 ~0.7% (fissile) [March 2026 · India–Canada: Carney visit, Cameco uranium deal and agreements]
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct: option **(3)**.
1: exploration across **15 states**; **Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor** at **Kalpakkam**.
2: **CIRUS** — India's **second** reactor, **1950s**; **RAPP** (Rajasthan) in **1960s**.
3: uranium atomic number **92**; **U-235** fissile, **U-238** fertile.
xa: **U-238 ~99.3%**, **U-235 ~0.7%**; ore **Uraninite (Pitchblende)**.
⚠ Power reactors use **3–5% enriched** LEU.
Three-stage programme (**Homi Bhabha**) ultimately aims at **thorium**.

66.s:
Assertion (A): The 1973 Oil Price Crisis was associated with the creation of the International Energy Agency.
Reason (R): The crisis was the first major use of oil as a geopolitical weapon.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
66.x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true: the crisis was followed by the creation of the International Energy Agency and represented the first major use of oil as a geopolitical weapon. However, the latter fact does not explain the institutional creation of the IEA.
66.tq: Assertion-Reason · tests the “Nature and outcome of the 1973 crisis” angle
n: First major use of oil as a geopolitical weapon; prices rose ~fourfold (~400%, 1973–74) → stagflation [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
Outcomes: petrodollar system; strategic petroleum reserves; creation of International Energy Agency (IEA) [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: outcomes of the 1973 crisis included the creation of the **International Energy Agency (IEA)**.
R is true: it was the **first major use** of oil as a **geopolitical weapon**.
xa: Trigger: **Arab members of OPEC** imposed an **oil embargo** on supporters of **Israel** in the **Yom Kippur War (1973)**.
Prices rose ~**fourfold** (~**400%**, **1973–74**) → **stagflation**.
Other outcomes: **petrodollar system** and **strategic petroleum reserves**.
⚠ 1973 = **political embargo**; present crisis = **physical disruption** of supply routes.

66.s:
In the context of the 1973 Oil Price Crisis and the disruption of oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz in April 2026, consider the following statements:

2. Arab members of OPEC imposed an oil embargo on countries opposing Israel in the Yom Kippur War.
3. The Yom Kippur War associated with the 1973 crisis took place in 1979.
66.x: Only statement 1 is correct. The West Asia conflict disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and prompted comparisons with 1973; the 1973 embargo targeted countries supporting Israel, and the associated war was in 1973, not 1979.
66.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Cause of the 1973 Oil Crisis” angle
n: West Asia conflict disrupted oil flows through Strait of Hormuz — comparisons with 1973 Oil Crisis [April 2026 · 1973 Oil Price Crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruption]

106.s:
Consider the following statements about heritage discoveries and returned antiquities in May 2026:
1. Kumbhalgarh Fort has the world's second-largest surviving defensive wall after the Great Wall of China.
2. The Dwarka underwater finds included Roman coins, pottery and Roman-inscribed stones.
3. The Netherlands returned 11th-century Chola Anaimangalam copper plates.
106.x: All three statements are correct. Kumbhalgarh's wall extends over 36 km, the Dwarka finds indicate India–Rome maritime trade, and the Netherlands returned the 11th-century Chola Anaimangalam copper plates.
106.tq: Multi-Statement Correctness · tests the “Monuments and antiquities” angle
n: Item: Kumbhalgarh Fort (Rajsamand, Rajasthan); Fact: ⚠ World's second-largest surviving defensive wall after Great Wall of China — 36+ km ("Great Wall of India"); built 15th c. by Mewar ruler Rana Kumbha in Aravallis; birthplace of Maharana Pratap; part of Hill Forts of Rajasthan (UNESCO 2013, with Chittorgarh, Ranthambore, Amer, Jaisalmer, Gagron) [May 2026 · History, heritage and culture — May 2026]

Item: Dwarka underwater finds (Gujarat); Fact: ASI found fort-like structure, Roman coins, pottery, Roman-inscribed stones off Bet Dwarka (Shankhodhar Island), Arabian Sea — India–Rome maritime trade; ASI DG Yadubir Singh Rawat [May 2026 · History, heritage and culture — May 2026]

Item: Leiden Plates; Fact: Netherlands returned 11th-century Chola Anaimangalam copper plates (21 large + 3 small, ~30 kg, bronze ring with Chola seal) — kept at Leiden University; India sought them since 2012 [May 2026 · History, heritage and culture — May 2026]
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct: option **(3)**.
**Kumbhalgarh Fort** has the world's **second-largest** surviving wall after the **Great Wall of China**.
**Dwarka** finds: **Roman coins**, pottery, Roman-inscribed stones; the **Netherlands** returned the **11th-century** Chola **Anaimangalam** plates.
xa: Kumbhalgarh wall: **36+ km**; built **15th c.** by **Rana Kumbha**.
The **Leiden Plates**: **21** large + **3** small, ~**30 kg**; India sought them since **2012**.
The Dwarka finds were off **Bet Dwarka (Shankhodhar Island)**.
